note: Cold War-shaped relations.
Non-aligned: on cordial terms with both blocs and neither's client.
Bonn's warmth here is what makes its later push for recognition bite.

Brazil: friendly with everyone and committed to nobody. The 1980s debt crisis is what Washington means to Brasilia, so the warmth is real but thin, and the Latin American nuclear rivalry with Argentina ended at Guadalajara in 1991.

Indonesia: an anti-communist client of the West since 1965, and Japan's largest aid recipient. Relations with Beijing were suspended outright in 1967 over the coup and are only restored in August 1990 — which is why they start negative and have to be repaired.

Egypt post-Camp David: the peace with Israel is cold but eleven years old, and it bought Cairo a permanent American subsidy. The suspension from the Arab League ended in 1989 and Egypt sits with Iraq in the Arab Cooperation Council as the game opens — Cairo's turn against Baghdad in August is a choice the sim has to make, not a fact it starts with.

Israel: the American relationship is the deepest in the game. Moscow broke relations in 1967 and does not restore them until October 1991, even as it lets its Jews leave. Ankara is the one Muslim capital with full ties.

Turkey in NATO: forty years in the alliance, two million of its people working in Germany, and Incirlik. Baghdad is a customer, not a friend — the Kirkuk-Yumurtalik pipeline is Iraq's main outlet and Ozal shuts it in August 1990.
Nigeria: Commonwealth ties to London, oil ties to Washington, and the non-aligned habits of a country that has led African diplomacy since independence.

Vietnam post-Cambodia: the last troops came home in September 1989 but nothing has been forgiven. Washington's embargo is fifteen years old and has four more to run; Beijing fought a border war in 1979, kept shelling into 1988, and sank three Vietnamese ships off Johnson Reef that March. Moscow is the patron whose money stops arriving this year.

Spain, four years into the European Community and eight into NATO. Warm with the Community it joined on 1 January 1986 and whose structural funds were rebuilding it, and warm-but-reserved with Washington: the 1988 base agreement was a renegotiation that expelled the 401st Tactical Fighter Wing from Torrejon, which is why the number here sits below Italy's 60 rather than beside it.

London is the outlier and Gibraltar is the reason. The Brussels Declaration of 1984 reopened the frontier and opened a negotiating process that went nowhere; the two are NATO allies who do not agree about a border. A positive but thin line, which is the shape of a grievance that is real and is never going to be a war.
Latin America is the other axis of Spanish foreign policy in this period — the first Ibero-American Summit met at Guadalajara in July 1991 on a Spanish initiative.

Canada in January 1990 is the most closely tied nation on this board to the most powerful one, and the 85 with Washington is the highest single number in this file. NORAD had put continental air defence under a joint command since 1958, the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement had been in force since 1 January 1989, and the two are NATO allies with a Canadian mechanised brigade and air division standing in Germany. Nothing else Canada has comes close, and much of Canadian foreign policy in this period is an attempt to have something else.

Paris is the exception among the Western capitals and Quebec is the whole of the reason. De Gaulle's 'Vive le Quebec libre' from the balcony of Montreal city hall in 1967 was a French head of state endorsing the breakup of a NATO ally on its own soil, and France has maintained a direct relationship with Quebec City ever since. Entered at 40, below Germany and Japan - which looks like an odd ranking until you remember that the Canadian brigade was at Lahr and Baden-Soellingen and that Japan was the second-largest customer.

Delhi is the coldest line Canada has with a democracy and it is 15 rather than 60 for two specific reasons. India's 1974 test used plutonium from the CIRUS reactor Canada had supplied for civil research, and Canada cut off nuclear cooperation over it. And Air India 182 was blown out of the sky off Ireland in June 1985 by a bomb loaded in Vancouver - the largest mass murder in Canadian history, and still being prosecuted twenty years later.

The Commonwealth pair are stated here so that they are stated once: Australia 70 and New Zealand 65 are shared institutions, a shared head of state, and no shared interest urgent enough to make either number higher.

Australia's alliance is real and unqualified: ANZUS in force, and the joint facilities at Pine Gap and Nurrungar doing work for the United States that no other ally's territory did. 78 rather than Canada's 85 only because there is no NORAD and no free trade agreement, not because there is any doubt.

Japan at 62 records something people forget about 1990: Japan had been Australia's largest export market since 1966, and the iron ore of the Pilbara and the coking coal of the Bowen Basin went almost entirely there. The economic relationship overtook the imperial one two decades before the sentimental one caught up, which is why this number sits within six points of Britain's.

China at 35 is a relationship in its worst state since recognition in 1972. Hawke wept on national television reading the casualty reports from Beijing on 9 June 1989 and extended the visas of some 42,000 Chinese students already in Australia, which Beijing treated as Beijing treats such things.

Indonesia at 42 is cooperative and squalid in equal measure. Australia was the only Western state to recognise the annexation of East Timor de jure, and Gareth Evans and Ali Alatas signed the Timor Gap Treaty dividing the seabed on 11 December 1989 - in a light aircraft circling over the Timor Sea, because there was no agreed coastline to sign it on. A working relationship between two states that do not like each other, which is what a number in the forties is for.

France at 12 is the atmospheric testing at Mururoa, which Australia and New Zealand jointly took to the International Court of Justice in 1973. Entered well above New Zealand's negative figure because Australia's grievance is a policy and New Zealand's is a killing, and because the Matignon Accords of 1988 had defused New Caledonia, which was the other half of it.

This block exists for one number. New Zealand and the United States open at 20 - below New Zealand and China, and only five above New Zealand and the Soviet Union - and that is neither a mistake nor a modelling choice. The Fourth Labour Government banned nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered warship visits, refused the USS Buchanan in February 1985, and Washington formally suspended its ANZUS security obligations to New Zealand in August 1986: downgraded from ally to friend, intelligence sharing cut, ministerial contact suspended. The ban was entrenched in the New Zealand Nuclear Free Zone, Disarmament, and Arms Control Act 1987, and by 1990 both major parties had accepted it. Two democracies of nearly identical outlook, and the alliance between them is switched off. A roster that means to cover the world has to be able to hold that, and a hand-enumerated table of blocs cannot.

France at -30 is the only negative number any of these three nations carries, and it is the Rainbow Warrior. Two DGSE agents bombed a Greenpeace vessel at its berth in Auckland Harbour on 10 July 1985 and killed the photographer Fernando Pereira - a state attack on a civilian target in the port of a friendly country. They were convicted of manslaughter, transferred to the French base at Hao under a UN-brokered settlement, and returned to France early in breach of it, the last of them in May 1988. Eighteen months before the game starts.

Britain at 62 is warm and diminished, and 1973 is why: the United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community and New Zealand lost the guaranteed access for butter and lamb that had been most of its economy since refrigerated shipping began in 1882. The relationship survived it. The trade did not.

Australia at 85 is stated in the Australian block above and not repeated here. It is the only alliance New Zealand has left, and Closer Economic Relations since 1983 makes it an economic union in all but name.
